summary:
The problem
Landing at the Moon’s south pole is hard because of two questions. Will the Sun be up to power the lander? And can the lander see Earth to talk to mission control? At the pole, the Sun skims the horizon and circles it over about 29.5 days. A hill only a degree or two tall can leave a site dark for weeks, and with no atmosphere, dark means extreme cold and no power. Earth also hovers near the horizon, so communication comes and goes.

NASA’s tools, such as Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, can answer this, but they’re built for specialists. Comparing sites and dates is slow, especially when a launch slips.

What we built

LunarLook is a web app that makes the comparison visual. Pick up to three landing sites, including Apollo sites, IM-2, and candidate polar regions, or enter your own coordinates, then choose a date. Each site gets a horizon view showing the Sun and Earth, a 30-day timeline showing when power and communication overlap, and key numbers like time until sunset and an overall rating.

Honest limits

It’s a prototype. The positions come from standard astronomical formulas, accurate to about a fraction of a degree, and should be checked against JPL Horizons. The terrain is a stand-in, not real LOLA data, which is the next step.

Why it matters

LunarLook turns a specialist’s question into something planners, teachers and students can understand in seconds.
details:
What it does and how it works

LunarLook is a web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates quickly. The user picks up to three sites (Apollo sites, Chandrayaan-3, IM-2, Chang’e 4, candidate south pole regions, or custom coordinates) and a landing date and time.

For each site, the app shows:

  • Sky view: the Sun and Earth plotted against the horizon, with their paths over the next 48 hours.
  • 30-day timeline: when the Sun is up, when Earth is visible, and when both are true (the operating window).
  • Key metrics: time until sunset or Earthset, percentage of time sunlit and with direct-to-Earth contact, longest period of darkness, a relative power estimate, and an overall rating.

Under the hood, the app calculates the Moon’s and Sun’s positions with analytical astronomical formulas, applies the Moon’s libration (wobble) to find where Earth and the Sun sit overhead on the lunar surface, and converts that to elevation and azimuth at the chosen site, including Earth parallax. There is no atmospheric refraction, matching the Moon’s conditions. A terrain horizon then decides whether each body is actually visible.

Benefits

  • Compares sites and dates in seconds instead of juggling multiple specialist tools.
  • Shows the effect of a launch delay (for example, one week) immediately.
  • Makes the extreme south pole lighting and communication environment easy to understand.
  • Runs in a single web page with no installation, server or account.

Intended impact

To speed up decisions when schedules or sites change, help science and engineering teams discuss trade-offs using the same visuals, and give students and the public a clear view of why lunar missions are so difficult.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas for the sky view and timelines, with no external libraries
  • Hardware: a standard laptop and browser
  • Method: Meeus-style lunar and solar position formulas with optical libration
  • Development: built with AI assistance from Claude (Anthropic). [Edit this line to match how your team actually worked.]

Creativity

Instead of tables of ephemeris data, LunarLook turns the problem into a picture: a horizon with the Sun and Earth moving across it, and color-coded strips that show the operating window at a glance. Scrubbing time, pressing Play, and jumping the date by a week let users feel how small changes have large effects.

Factors considered

  • Audience range: planners, educators and the public, with a plain-language explainer built in.
  • Speed: results update instantly with no loading or setup.
  • Accuracy and honesty: the positions are accurate to roughly a fraction of a degree, good for scouting but not flight design. The terrain horizon is currently a synthetic profile, not real LOLA data, and the app says so on the page.
  • Physical realism: no atmosphere, libration, Earth parallax, and the Sun’s disk size.
  • Future work: load real LOLA horizon masks, validate against JPL Horizons, and add a “best landing day” finder.
